opus-5.5.text:
I think the progress over the past two years has been faster than most people expected, but the direction has also become clearer.

Two years ago, the main story was scaling pre-training: more data, more compute, bigger models, and you get better next-token prediction, which gives you broad general knowledge and decent language ability. That still matters, but I don't think it's the main driver of the most important improvements anymore.

The biggest change, in my view, is that models have learned to *think* and to *act*. With reinforcement learning on top of strong base models, especially on tasks where you can verify the result, like math and coding, models now reason over long horizons, try things, check themselves, and recover from mistakes. That's qualitatively different from a model that just produces a fluent answer in one shot.

The second change is agents. A model that can use tools, write and run code, search, and operate over many steps is no longer just a chatbot. It starts to do real work. When you can give a model a task that takes a human hours, and it completes a meaningful portion of it autonomously, the value it creates changes by an order of magnitude.

Third, long context has gone from a nice feature to infrastructure. A lot of what we bet on early was that being able to process very long inputs, and later very long trajectories of reasoning and actions, would be fundamental. I think that has been validated. Long-horizon reasoning and agentic tasks essentially *are* long-context problems.

If I had to summarize: the past two years moved us from "models that know a lot" to "models that can figure things out." The bottleneck is shifting. It's less about raw data, since high-quality human data is limited, and more about how to create good environments, good reward signals, and let the model generate its own experience to learn from.

There are still clear gaps. Generalization from verifiable domains to open-ended ones is not solved. Reliability over very long tasks is still not where it needs to be. And I'd say we're still early on models that continuously learn. But overall, I'm more optimistic now than I was two years ago. The path to much more capable systems looks more concrete, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can use tools and code to complete a meaningful portion of tasks that take a human hours, but it does not state that models can work continuously for several hours on a complex coding task.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the past two years have been both more and less than people expected, depending on which axis you look at.

If you look at raw capability, the progress has been remarkable. Two years ago the frontier was essentially about scaling pretraining: more data, more compute, bigger models, and you got predictable gains on benchmarks. What changed is that pretraining alone started to saturate, not because scaling stopped working, but because high-quality data became the bottleneck. And the field found a second axis: reinforcement learning on top of these models, letting them think longer, verify their own reasoning, and improve on tasks where you can check the answer. That shift from "next-token prediction" to "learning from outcomes" is, in my view, the single most important development of this period. It took problems that looked hopeless, competition math, hard coding tasks, and made them tractable very quickly.

The second thing is that models went from being chat assistants to being agents. That sounds like a product change, but underneath it's a capability change. A model that can take fifty or a hundred actions in a row, use tools, recover from mistakes, and stay on task is fundamentally different from one that gives you a paragraph. Long-horizon reliability is where most of the real progress has gone, and it's also where the gap between models is now most visible.

Where it's been less than expected: generalization is still uneven. A model can solve an olympiad problem and then fail at something a human would consider trivial. The benchmarks moved faster than real-world economic impact. And we still don't have a clean theory of why RL generalizes in some domains and not others.

So if I had to summarize: the paradigm shifted, from scaling data to scaling the model's own thinking and interaction with the environment. I think that's the big story. And I suspect the next two years will be defined by how far that second paradigm can go before it needs its own successor.

astra-6.text:
I think we should look at two things: how capable the models are, and how much of that capability translates into useful work.

On the first, the progress has been substantial. We’ve moved from models that mainly produce plausible responses toward models that can handle more complicated instructions, write code, and work through problems over multiple steps. The interaction is becoming less about asking a question and getting an answer, and more about giving the model a task.

But the second is harder. A model can give an impressive demonstration and still be unreliable in everyday use. If it performs nine steps correctly and makes a mistake on the tenth, that can undermine the whole result. So I wouldn’t judge progress only by benchmarks or the best examples. I’d also ask: How often does it finish the task? How much supervision does it need? And what does it cost?

To me, the progress over these two years is real, but there’s still a considerable gap between having a powerful model and having a system you can consistently delegate work to. Closing that gap is a very important part of what comes next.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the progress has been substantial, but I’d separate it into two dimensions: how capable the models are, and how reliably those capabilities translate into useful work.

On the capability side, models have become much better at understanding instructions, writing code, and working through problems that require several steps. We’re moving from systems that mainly produce plausible answers toward systems that can tackle more complex tasks.

But reliability is still a major gap. A model can do something impressive once, yet struggle to do it consistently across different situations. For a user, that difference matters a lot. Can you give it a task and trust it to finish, or do you have to keep checking and correcting it?

So I wouldn’t judge progress only by benchmarks or a few impressive demonstrations. I’d also look at how much useful work a model can complete, how much human supervision it needs, and what that costs. The progress over the past two years is real; turning that capability into dependable productivity is still the central challenge.
